I've posted something like this before, but let's really stop and think about the (extremely complicated) process of "gentrification," which is always depicted as a bad or undesirable thing, with a fictional example. (I am not an economist so this won't be perfect.)

An American city has gone to shit. Nobody wants to live or have a business there anymore because of crime and poverty. (I think crime leads to poverty, not poverty to crime, but we don't have to agree on that for the purposes of this thought experiment.) This feels like a hopeless situation that will just continue to spiral out of control. People who can't afford to live elsewhere chose to live there anyway despite the risks, but it's not a great place to be, and people are constantly moving out as well.

Because the city is such an undesirable place to live, real estate prices and rent are being forced down to hopefully attract people to live and work there anyway. Eventually, the prices are so low that some enterprising small business owner looks at the situation and sees an opportunity to make money. A risky opportunity, but he knows that risk means he'll have less competition. "I can start a business in this city and serve the undeserved people in the area and really clean up if I play my cards right." The business owner may or may not care about the people living there, but he certainly wants to get richer, so he starts his new business.

Other businesses also move into the area to serve the population because of the low real estate prices, and they provide jobs to the locals as well as services. Gradually, this helps to raise the desirability of being in the city, and that makes real estate/housing prices go up as demand rises for residency there. The city is starting to once again become a place that people with options want to be.

Unfortunately, the people who moved in years ago because of the very low housing costs don't like that things are changing. The one difference they notice the most easily and feel the most sharply is the rising cost of rent. Crime is dropping too as opportunity rises (and as police presence increases to protect the new businesses), but that's not as easy to notice in your everyday life. Some of these people decide to move out and rent somewhere cheaper even though they think of the city as "home." For everyone else who can afford to move in or to stay, the resources and opportunities that come with more business in the area are starting to pay off.

This process continues gradually. Housing prices, and the general cost of living, continues to rise as more businesses enter the area and offer more (and better) jobs. People who can't afford the new prices move out and find places that are more affordable for them, and new people who can afford the higher prices move in to be in a now bustling city.

The above is an (again, simplified) example of gentrification. At every step along the way, people are making voluntary choices about what's best for them. This happens organically, efficiently, and without any central planning or the use of force.

Why would critics of gentrification oppose this process? A rising cost of living in a particular place is inherently tied to how well the city is doing. If the city starts doing better, then it will cost more to live there, and that means some people will have to move out. So what?

Everybody can understand the desire not to leave the place you've called home for a long time. It can be hard, emotionally, do to it. But no central boogeyman is making it happen in this process> Instead, it's a natural consequence of the city becoming healthier as everyone makes individual choices about what's best for them. It's not "mean" to expect people to take care of themselves and to make those choices even if it's difficult or unpleasant.

Are critics of gentrification saying that a terrible city with people living in it should stay a terrible place to live? We don't ever hear the critics saying that exactly because they would be ridiculed and ignored, but they are effectively saying that by getting angry over gentrification. It's just that they don't understand that rising prices are directly related to higher demand.

Oh, wait a second. Most of the people moving out happen to be black, and most of the people moving in happen to be white. So that's why it's a problem? Even though we've already explained how the basic dynamics of gentrification are driven by healthy self-interest, now the left makes the same unprovable claims they always make that gentrification is really about racism. They don't specify what that means exactly or explain how bigotry could be a driving force behind gentrification, but they don't like the changing color of the city, and at the very least it kills them that someone in the city might be enjoying the demographic change a little too much, so: "racism!!!"

And since the left won't let anyone discuss the many reasons (and I don't just mean IQ) for rough economic stratification between ethnic groups, they're free to claim "racism" forever and misrepresent a complex but positive phenomenon with, essentially, a slur. A problem created and perpetuated by the very same "caring," "compassionate" people. Lovely.

TL;DR version: "gentrification" is what naturally happens when a place improves and current residents can't afford to live there anymore. Moving really fucking sucks, but gentrification is an unavoidable side effect of the best case scenario.
